summary:
Earth4Space is an interactive website created by our team, ApesInSpace, to explore how different places on Earth compare to potential landing sites and future base locations on the Moon and Mars. We use publicly available data from NASA, other space agencies and scientific databases to compare features such as geology, terrain, topography and environmental conditions.

Through the website, users can explore different locations on the Moon and Mars, compare them with places on Earth and discover potential analogue sites. The Analogue Finder allows users to select specific parameters and see how closely different Earth locations match their chosen planetary site. Users can also explore analogue locations that are already being studied, as well as less-explored areas that could be worth investigating in the future.

We developed Earth4Space to make scientific data easier to access, understand and compare, especially for people interested in space exploration. By identifying places on Earth that share similar characteristics with the Moon and Mars, we hope to help researchers find suitable locations for testing equipment, technologies and mission procedures before they are used in space. This could make future missions safer, more practical and less expensive.
details:
1. What is Earth4Space and how does it work?

Earth4Space is a website used to find places on Earth that are similar to parts of the Moon and Mars.

Users can explore different lunar and Martian locations, look at existing Earth analogue sites and search for new possibilities. With the Analogue Finder, users can choose the characteristics they want to compare and see which places on Earth are the closest matches. Results are shown as percentage matches, making it easier to compare and rank different locations.

Our database currently includes 45 Earth locations and six reference sites on the Moon and Mars.

2. Why use Earth4Space?

Finding scientific information about Earth, the Moon and Mars often means searching through many different websites and databases. We wanted to bring this information together in one place.

Earth4Space makes it easier to compare different environments and discover places on Earth that could be useful for future space research, including locations that have not been widely explored as possible analogues.

3. Our Goal

We want to help scientists and researchers prepare for future missions to the Moon and Mars.

Before sending equipment and astronauts into space, it is important to test technologies and exploration methods here on Earth. By finding more places that resemble parts of these planetary environments, we hope to help create new opportunities for research and testing.

4. How did we create Earth4Space?

We built an interactive website using HTML, CSS and JavaScript, with help from Claude. We also created an Excel database to organise the information used in our comparisons.

We collected information from open scientific resources, including:

  • NASA Planetary Data System (PDS): data from planetary missions.
  • NASA POWER: climate and environmental data.
  • NASA Earthdata and Worldview: satellite images and observations of Earth.
  • NASA Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter: information about the Moon's surface.
  • USGS: geological and topographical data.
  • SoilGrids: soil properties and composition.

These sources help us compare different features of Earth with those found on the Moon and Mars.

5. What makes Earth4Space different?

We didn't want to create just another list of places that are already known as Moon or Mars analogues.

Instead, we wanted users to be able to explore different possibilities themselves. They can choose the characteristics they are interested in, change the parameters and see how the results change.

This also gives us the opportunity to identify less-explored places on Earth that could be interesting for future research.

6. Which parameters do we compare?

We focused on features that can be meaningfully compared between Earth and the Moon or Mars.

These include:

  • Topography: elevation, slopes and terrain.
  • Geology: iron oxides, silica and rock composition.
  • Soil: pH, soluble salts and organic carbon.
  • Environment: aridity, rainfall, temperature variation and vegetation.
  • Research potential: existing studies, available data and suitability for field testing.

Users can select different combinations of these parameters depending on what they want to investigate.
